articles.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
articles.summary: A cyber extortion group called 'n0n' claims to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included campaign interactions for 'tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses'

blocks.text: JP MORGAN CHASE. People exit the JPMorgan Chase and Co., headquarters in New York City, USA, April 1, 2026.
Eduardo Munoz/Reuters
A cyber extortion group called 'n0n' claims to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included campaign interactions for 'tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses'

items: JPMorgan Chase confirmed a cyberattack targeting third-party vendors, potentially exposing customer marketing data including names and email addresses.
The bank experienced transaction processing issues earlier in the week due to a software bug, unrelated to the cyberattack, prompting inquiries from regulators.

A hacking group named 'n0n' claimed responsibility for the breach, affecting not only JPMorgan but also Visa and Mastercard, with data primarily related to marketing campaigns and customer information.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Thursday, November 19, that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding the company would be contacting affected customers directly.
“There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” the spokesperson added.
Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions.

These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft’s global email outage, while last month crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.

After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, according to a an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents.

“Customers don’t distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here,” said Carissa Robb at SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. “There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinizing the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared,” Robb said.

A cyber extortion group called “n0n” claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included “hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses,” according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.

The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data.
JPMorgan declined to comment on the data.
The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data.

A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses — non-payments information — from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.”

The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review. Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data.
The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses.
The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. – Rappler.com

NSW health issues public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas

Three people who lost consciousness and…

blocks.text: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials have said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free…

blocks.text: Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist, associate professor Nicholas Evans, said on Friday Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but ultimately, Evans told the court, it was most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”

Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they don’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks, because it’s so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times that she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.

blocks.text: Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany on Friday, November 20:
November 20, 2026
Lufthansa to slash 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt, Munich — reports
German flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.
The timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

Lufthansa's parent company Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.
In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

articles.title: AFP opens 2026 DAGITPA exercise with external defense focus
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday opened the 10th iteration of its Dagat, Langit at Lupa (DAGITPA) exercise, with a focus on strengthening the country's external defense and…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 2:38pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday opened the 10th iteration of its Dagat, Langit at Lupa (DAGITPA) exercise, with a focus on strengthening the country's external defense and territorial integrity.

AFP chief General Antonio Nafarrete said the exercise aims to test the military's ability to conduct joint operations under realistic conditions, bringing together the capabilities of its different services.

"This security environment we face today requires an armed forces that can respond to threats to our sovereignty and territorial integrity," Nafarrete said during the opening ceremony at Camp Aguinaldo.

"This requires more than the capabilities of our individual services. We must be able to bring these capabilities together, make timely decisions, and carry out operations as one joint force," he added.
For Nafarrete, DAGITPA should be treated as a “mission rehearsal” rather than just another military exercise.

The exercise, known as AJEX DAGITPA 10-2026, is designed to enhance the AFP's ability to address current and emerging security challenges, particularly those involving territorial defense, maritime security, and cyber defense.

This exercise integrates the Philippine Army, Philippine Navy, Philippine Air Force, and Special Operations Forces to improve their capabilities in carrying out joint operations across land, sea, and air domains.

AJEX DAGITPA 10-2026 is scheduled from November 17 to 27, with major activities taking place within the joint operational areas of the Northern Luzon Command, Western Command, and National Capital Region Command.
The exercise has four major lines of effort: Command and Control Exercise, Field Training Exercise (FTX), Sustainment Exercise, and Humanitarian Civic Assistance.
FTX will cover three operational areas including Northern Luzon, West, and the National Capital Region.
Among the activities are integrated air and missile defense, air-sea battle, joint maritime strikes, maritime key terrain security operations, and counter-landing live-fire exercises.

For the defense of the West, the AFP will conduct operations focused on protecting sea lines of communication, securing offshore energy infrastructure, and testing anti-access and area denial capabilities.
Key areas include the Balabac Strait, Mindoro Strait, Pag-asa Island, and the offshore Nido Platform.

The exercise will also integrate cyber defense and information warfare scenarios to test the military's ability to respond to cyber-enabled threats and evolving disinformation campaigns. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
articles.summary: Nigeria's proposed reform follows years of calls from psychiatrists and a parallel Senate bill.

blocks.text: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.
"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.
Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.
Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.
Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.
Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Hontiveros quote on driving Dutertes out of politics is fake
articles.summary: The senator did not make the statement attributed to her, nor has she officially declared a 2028 presidential run

blocks.text: Claim: Senator Risa Hontiveros said that if she wins the 2028 presidential election, she will ensure that members of the Duterte family are removed from politics.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook user named “Solid Sara Du30 supporter’s 2028” posted a quote card that has garnered 1,100 reactions, 1,700 comments, and 47 shares as of writing.
The quote attributed to Hontiveros reads, “Kapag ako mananalo, sisiguraduhin [kong] mawawala ang lahat ng mga Duterte sa politika, pangako ko ‘yan.”
(If I win, I will ensure that all the Dutertes are removed from politics — that is my promise.)
Several social media users believed the quote to be genuine, with some questioning Hontiveros’ winnability while others said their loyalties lie with the Duterte family.
The facts: Hontiveros did not make such a statement. No official records or reports show that she said this.

Although the senator has not officially declared a 2028 presidential run, she stated in interviews that she is open to serving as the unified candidate for the opposition against Vice President Sara Duterte, who in February announced her intent to run for president in 2028.
In an August press conference in Iloilo, Hontiveros said that the opposition is still undecided on who to put forward as its presidential bet.
“We are now in the decision-making process… I am preparing very hard, working very hard para maging ‘yung pipiliin ng hanay namin as the strongest possible candidate sa 2028,” she said.
(We are now in the decision-making process… I am preparing very hard, working very hard to be the one chosen by our side as the strongest possible candidate for 2028.)

She then said that if chosen, she would talk to allies to gain their support. Hontiveros added, “Importante na isa lang. Let’s unite around the strongest one para may fighting chance tayo and we can make the best offer sa ating mga kababayan.”
(It is important that there is only one candidate. Let’s unite around the strongest candidate so that we have a fighting chance and can present the best offer to our countrymen.)
Several groups are already rallying in support of Hontiveros, presenting her as an alternative to traditional politicians who currently dominate the government.

Presidential preference polls: In a September pre-election survey released by Pulse Asia, Duterte still leads the presidential preference list with 50% of respondents choosing her. Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo followed at 26%, Senator Raffy Tulfo at 12%, and Hontiveros at 3%.

Data visualized by Rappler showed that Duterte is a frontrunner in numerous presidential poll results as of early 2026. However, past elections suggest that being the top contender in pre-election surveys does not guarantee victory. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Fact check: Facebook reel twists survey findings on Sara Duterte impeachment
articles.summary: Facebook page Facts PH misrepresents Momentum Research survey figures to falsely claim most Filipinos believe Sara Duterte is guilty.

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 2:22pm
A Facebook reel misrepresents Momentum Research’s survey findings on public opinion of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment.
Facts PH / Screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — A Facebook reel misrepresents the findings of a public opinion research firm on the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Facebook page Facts PH shared a reel misrepresenting Momentum Research’s survey findings on Sara Duterte’s impeachment.
Screenshot taken Nov. 20, 2026, 1:40 p.m.
In a November 18 reel, Facebook page Facts PH attributed supposed findings to Momentum Research’s “latest” survey on whether Duterte is “guilty” or “innocent.”
The reel claimed that 64% of participants believed the vice president is guilty, while 23% allegedly said she is innocent.
Support for the prosecution also allegedly jumped from 26% to 38%, while support for the defense dropped to 17%, it added.
The post’s caption read:
Is public confidence in Sara Duterte’s defense fading? A new Momentum Research study reveals a growing divide: 64% of participants believe Duterte is guilty, while only 23% believe she is innocent.
Rating: This is false.
Facts
Momentum Research did not release any study stating 64% of participants believe the vice president is “guilty,” contrary to what the Facebook reel says.
Momentum Research’s October survey found varying levels of public acceptance for possible conviction or acquittal verdicts in Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

In its November 10 Facebook post, the firm published its October findings on public acceptance of potential impeachment court verdicts. The survey found that 32% would only accept the decision if it is to convict Duterte, 24% would only accept an acquittal, while 27% would accept either verdict.
Momentum Research’s October survey found that 38.8% of Filipino adults believe Sara Duterte should be convicted, while 33.8% believe she should be acquitted.
Momentum Research / Website
Meanwhile, 38.8% of Filipino adults believe Duterte should be convicted, while 33.8% believe she should be acquitted, according to its October 2026 National Momentum Survey.

There are no 64% or 23% figures in Momentum Research's published findings on whether Sara Duterte is considered “guilty” or “innocent.” The firm also makes no mention of these specific figures in relation to public opinion on the possible verdicts of the impeachment court.
Momentum Research’s August survey found that 64% of respondents agree or strongly agree that Duterte should return the P73 million in confidential funds disallowed by the Commission on Audit.
The figures cited in the Facebook reel appear to have been taken from the firm’s August 2026 survey on whether the vice president should return the Commission on Audit-disallowed confidential funds.
In the firm’s study, 64% agree or strongly agree that Duterte should return the P73 million in confidential funds, while 24% disagree or strongly disagree.
The same survey found that 23.3% of respondents believe Duterte’s defense team is outperforming the prosecution, while 15.2% say the prosecution is doing a better job.
Momentum Research / Facebook
In the same August survey, 23.3% believe Duterte's defense team is outperforming the prosecution, while 15.2% see the prosecution doing a better job.
These findings do not support the reel’s claim that the prosecution was gaining more support than the defense.
Why we fact-checked this
Friday, November 20, marks the 45th day of the vice president's impeachment proceedings, with the defense presenting more witnesses.
The impeachment trial currently centers on Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, concerning alleged unexplained wealth and failure to properly declare assets.
As of November 20, the Facebook reel has garnered more than 2,200 views and 30 reactions.

articles.title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges
articles.summary:
Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme

An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four…

blocks.text: An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.

The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.
The issue dates back to November 2023 when the children’s school, Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, held a non-uniform fundraising day for Children in Need.

The four children, all British Muslims aged between six and 10 at the time, attended wearing items displaying Palestinian colours or the Palestinian flag, in memory of children who had been killed in Gaza and those who continued to suffer during the conflict, which was ongoing at the time.
One child wore a Children in Need Pudsey sticker featuring a bow tie in Palestinian colours. Another wore a homemade badge bearing the Palestinian flag and colours.
Parents of the four children said they had repeatedly asked the school to apologise for their treatment of the children and had launched a legal challenge when none was forthcoming.

At a hearing at Central London county court on Thursday, the court heard that the academy trust had now made a formal apology to the children and their families and would pay them substantial compensation.

Lawyers for the children alleged direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment on grounds including race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of thought, conscience and belief.

Shahid Achhala, the father of one of the children, said: “What happened to our son was deeply disturbing and should never have happened to any child. He was just eight years old, expressing compassion and solidarity with children suffering in Gaza, including members of his own extended family. Instead of being supported and protected by the school entrusted with his care, he was deliberately subjected to mistreatment that caused him considerable emotional distress.

“For almost three years, we have had to fight legally for accountability and an acknowledgment of the wrongs we believe were committed. While we welcome Lion Academy Trust’s apology, we cannot overlook the distress caused to our son and our family, or the fact that this matter could have been resolved long time ago.”
The families were represented by law firm Leigh Day and supported in their legal claim by Prevent Watch, which provides casework support to individuals and families affected by the Prevent duty.

Layla Aitlhadj, a director at Prevent Watch, said: “In this case, parents who were protecting their children’s rights were told that their concerns were ‘false and malicious’. They held firm through three years of pressure. Today the families, and the wider community who stood with them, have been vindicated.”
The academy trust has been approached for comment.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: ICC did not say arrest warrant vs Dela Rosa is fake
articles.summary: Contrary to the claim, the International Criminal Court has previously confirmed the issuance of an arrest warrant against Senator Bato Dela Rosa

blocks.text: Claim: The International Criminal Court (ICC) said that the arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is fake.

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel bearing the claim has already received 1.3 million views, 10,000 shares, and 2,800 comments as of writing. It was posted on November 8 and continues to gain traction up to this date.
The text overlaid on the video reads, “ICC na nagsabi na hindi wanted si Bato bakit ang Pilipinas gusto [mahuli] si Bato may 50 million pa.”
(The ICC has stated that Bato is not a wanted person. Why, then, does the Philippines want to capture him with a 50-million [peso] bounty?)

The video also shows a photo of ICC Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner holding a document labeled “confirmed fake.” Photos of Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag, and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. are also featured in the video.
More text overlaid on the video reads, “Bulabog na! Shocking! ICC kumanta na! Hindi wanted si Bato! Yari kayo ngayon!”
(Chaotic! Shocking! The ICC has finally spoken! Bato isn’t a wanted man! You’re in big trouble now!)

The facts: Contrary to the claim, the ICC has previously confirmed the issuance of an arrest warrant against Dela Rosa. The ICC has not made any official statement on its website or status conferences saying that the arrest warrant is fake, or that Dela Rosa was not being sought by law enforcement under an active warrant.
The warrant remains active and can be accessed through the official ICC website. It was originally issued as secret in November 2025 and was only unsealed in May 2026.

Dela Rosa is alleged to have committed a crime against humanity of murder and of being among the perpetrators of the drug war under former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is currently detained in The Hague, Netherlands.

The international tribunal said that Dela Rosa, as Duterte’s police chief during his administration, knew about the operations and the scope of the war on drugs, created a network of perpetrators, controlled a structure of power, encouraged killings as part of the campaign, and threatened the ICC and fuelled disinformation about the drug war.
In hiding: Dela Rosa is currently in hiding, with a P50 million bounty offered for his arrest.

He was last seen at the Senate in May, appearing after months of absence from the chamber in a surprise move to cast his vote in a leadership coup against former Senate president Tito Sotto. At the time, the ICC had already publicized the arrest warrant against him. Dela Rosa then reportedly escaped from the Senate premises on May 14.

Previous fact checks: Rappler has fact-checked posts falsely claiming an invalidated arrest warrant against Dela Rosa. In November alone, at least three false claims — including the Supreme Court’s supposed dismissal of the warrant, a fake quote card of Dela Rosa denying the existence of the warrant, and a misused old video of Remulla saying no such warrant exists — have been debunked.
Other false claims about Dela Rosa have also been fact-checked:

items: FACT CHECK: No reports of Trump wanting to talk to Dela Rosa
FACT CHECK: ‘Shoot-to-kill’ Bato dela Rosa warning by Lordan Suan is fake
FACT CHECK: No basis for claim that Bato Dela Rosa is under Trump’s protection
FACT CHECK: Bato dela Rosa not yet arrested; online posts misuse old video
FACT CHECK: Bato dela Rosa not at recent INC rallies; post uses January 2025 video

blocks.text: – Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com
Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Overlooked Apayao flower identified as new plant species
articles.summary: Scientists identify the plant as Medinilla bulutiorum, a species new to science from the forests of Calanasan, Apayao

blocks.text: FLOWER FIND. Medinilla bulutiorum, a newly identified flowering plant from Calanasan, Apayao, grows in the province's lower montane forests.
courtesy of Jiro T. Adorador
Scientists identify the plant as Medinilla bulutiorum, a species new to science from the forests of Calanasan, Apayao

items: A new plant species, Medinilla bulutiorum, has been identified in the forests of Calanasan, Apayao, marking a significant botanical discovery.
The species, which belongs to the Melastomataceae family, was published in the journal Phytotaxa and is notable for its distinct characteristics compared to similar plants.
This discovery highlights the biodiversity of Calanasan's forests and the importance of ongoing botanical exploration, with three new species documented since 2025.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
BAGUIO, Philippines – It was not hiding. In fact, the flowering plant is common in the forest where researchers found it. Yet botanists had overlooked it for centuries.
Now, a team of scientists has officially identified the plant as Medinilla bulutiorum, a species new to science from the forests of Calanasan, Apayao.

The “discovery,” published Wednesday, November 18, in the international scientific journal Phytotaxa, adds another species to the growing list of botanical finds from a province whose forests continue to reveal how much remains undocumented.
Researchers recorded the plant in Barangay Eva Puzon, where it grows in lower montane forests at elevations of approximately 700 to 900 meters.

The study was authored by Jiro T. Adorador, Zhereeleen D. Meneses-Adorador, Breiden Dela Cruz, Sarah Mae C. Batil, Jayson C. Ibañez, and J. Peter Quakenbush, who are affiliated with the University of the Philippines Los Baños, Apayao’s provincial and municipal environment offices, the Philippine Eagle Foundation, and Grand Valley State University in the United States.
The newly described species belongs to the Melastomataceae family, which includes the familiar ornamental Medinilla magnifica.

Both plants produce long, hanging flower clusters with prominent bracts, but M. bulutiorum differs in several characteristics, including its smaller leaves, rounded branchlets, more crowded flower clusters, and brownish covering on parts of its inflorescence.
Its identification marks at least the third plant species newly described from Calanasan since 2025.
In October 2025, scientists published Vaccinium kilangensis, a relative of blueberries collected near Kilang Pass along the Apayao–Ilocos Norte boundary.
Another species, Medinilla calanasan, first encountered in Barangay Eva, was formally described in February 2026.
Three species described in just over a year point to the scientific importance of Calanasan’s forests, where systematic botanical exploration has been limited.
The researchers themselves noted that M. bulutiorum had gone unnoticed by botanists despite being widespread at the site where it was documented.

The species was named in honor of the Bulut family, particularly the late Elias K. Bulut Sr., known as EKB, in recognition of the family’s leadership and stewardship of ancestral lands. Bulut is regarded as a founding political figure of Apayao.
Despite the discovery, scientists still know relatively little about the plant’s overall population and geographical distribution.

Researchers have provisionally assessed it as data deficient under the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List criteria. The classification does not mean the species is endangered. It means available scientific information is insufficient to determine its extinction risk.
The discovery adds to the biological importance of the Apayaos Biosphere Reserve, which UNESCO recognized in July 2024.
Covering Apayao’s diverse landscapes, the reserve is internationally recognized for its biodiversity and efforts to balance conservation with the needs of local communities.

The latest findings also show why continued botanical surveys matter. Identifying a species allows researchers to study its distribution, assess potential threats, and determine what protection it may need.

For Calanasan, the succession of discoveries is more than a collection of new scientific names. It provides further evidence of the biological diversity of its forests and the importance of keeping those habitats intact.
Medinilla bulutiorum may have been familiar to people who have long lived near these forests. What is new is its formal recognition by science.
And with three species described from Calanasan since 2025, researchers have good reason to keep looking. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cale88 reduced employees due to non-operation, change of management -- DTI witness
articles.summary: Cale88 had reduced its number of employees from 2024 to 2025 due to a change in ownership, according to a defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) on Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:40pm
Cale88 reduced the number of employees from 2024 to 2025 due to a change in ownership, according to a defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) on Friday.
The food corporation was linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio, and had previously been flagged for having only two employees while generating P150 million in sales.

On the 45th day of Duterte’s impeachment trial, DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo of DTI’s Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group presented several documents regarding Cale88, one of which was a Plant Inspection Report.

The Plant Inspection Report detailed a visit by DTI Board of Investment (BOI) officials to Cale88 on May 18, 2026. It listed the company’s new owners as of 2026, namely a certain Lolita Paimalan as President, Chris Chiu as Legal Officer, and Leo Sacurom as a Compliance Officer.
“Ito po yung mga bagong may-ari, bagong presidente nung Cale88 Foods Corporation,” Rodolfo said.
(These are the new owners, the new president of Cale88 Foods Corporation.)

“During the inspection, the firm's compliance with its terms and conditions has been discussed, particularly, its direct labor commitment. For 2025, which is Year 3, the firm had to maintain direct labor of 39. Yun po kasi yung nakalagay doon sa kanyang specific terms and conditions na cinommit po sa atin sa gobyerno. But based on the 2025 BOI Form S-1, the firm had an actual labor of 50 while in 2024 they had reported 201,” Roldolfo said, reading the report.

“In response to the inquiry on the reduction of the number of labor from 2024 to 2025, the firm explained that it was attributable to a period of non-operation in 2025 due to the change in management and ownership,” he added.

Rodolfo explained that a change of ownership should be reported to the BOI. This report should include previous and current ownership structures, as well as the General Information Sheets before and after the change.

According to a separate DTI report titled “Report on Actual Date of Start of Commercial Operations, Initial Investments and Employment”, Cale88 officially began operations on January 1, 2023. It had 117 direct laborers and one person in admin and sales. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Kellie Sloane says she’s ‘pretty sure’ NSW Liberals exodus is over after Mark Speakman resigns
articles.summary:
Former NSW opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he became eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

A third of the 24 current Liberal MPs have announced they will not recontest their seat in March, including Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.
In a press conference on Friday, Sloane insisted the departures were not an indictment of the party’s election prospects.

“No, that’s not the truth. What we are seeing is an impressive cross section of abilities and talent and tenure in our party,” she told reporters in the same room where, exactly a year ago, Speakman announced he would resign as Liberal leader in her favour.
“We have people who have been in government before. We have people who have been in for a medium amount of time, and we’re going to have people with fresh ideas.”
Sloane said she had tried to convince Speakman to stay and said many of the MPs leaving had been in parliament for more than 10 years, although Lane is a first-term MP.
Sloane said a significant number of Liberals had retired before the 2023 election, in which the Coalition lost government and the party dropped nine seats.

Asked if she could guarantee that further MPs would not step down ahead of the March vote, Sloane said: “Look, I certainly hope not. I certainly hope not. I’m pretty sure that’s done. I’m pretty sure that’s done.”
Warnings against becoming ‘One Nation lite’
Since last year’s leadership spill, the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is now at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.
On Friday, Sloane rejected the claims from “anonymous names in a Financial Review article”, saying the Coalition only needed to flip six Labor seats to form minority government.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, said the Liberals faced an “existential threat” following a wipeout at the 2025 federal election and an “orange wave that seems to be coming across the country”.
He warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
after newsletter promotion
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced the former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.
On Friday, Sloane said Raffoul had been talking to her about Liberal party roles “only two months ago”.
“She’s decided to chase personal ambition. She’s a very ambitious person, but she’s changed sides, and that’s a decision Chris Minns has made.”

Earlier, the NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, rejected the idea that One Nation was pushing Labor to become “Liberal lite”, saying Raffoul’s candidacy reflected “a journey that I think many Liberal people are going through as well”.

articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
articles.summary:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment…

blocks.text: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”

blocks.caption: Polarisation has also hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres. Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

blocks.caption: The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

blocks.text: In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

blocks.caption: Russia has opposed the Argentine candidate Rafael Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP

blocks.text: In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

articles.title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
articles.summary:
Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in…
articles.byline: Ali Aziz, Maria Talal and Tom Levitt

blocks.text: The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”

The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.

articles.title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Investigation launched after details of grief and trauma uploaded, raising questions over extent of issue

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation…

blocks.text: The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers.

Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP.
Inquiries made by Rosanna under freedom of information laws revealed that her therapy notes had been accessed by staff who did not work at the hospital trust where she was being treated.

Her discovery led to her stopping the treatment she was receiving for bipolar disorder with South London and Maudsley NHS trust (SLaM). It meant she had no mental health support during a close family bereavement.

Rosanna’s case has prompted questions in parliament, and suggests many other patients’ psychotherapy notes, including those of children, could have been shared without their knowledge or consent. This week the ICO confirmed it would investigate the case after a request to expedite it by the former Labour minister Philip Hunt.
Her case also raises questions about whether the new single patient record, proposed under the health bill, will include intimate details from any psychotherapy sessions provided by the NHS.
SLaM said it was reviewing how it documented psychotherapy on electronic patient records and how it communicated how data was shared.

Rosanna’s psychotherapy notes were uploaded to the London Care Record (LCR), an electronic patient record accessible to up 140,000 NHS staff, at a time of increasing concern about health workers snooping on patients.

She said: “I felt horrified looking over my GP’s shoulder as they checked what I had told them about my therapy records being available on the LCR. It’s like discovering that your personal diary has been photocopied and placed in a library.”

SLaM said “no intimate details” from therapy sessions had been shared, but in a response to Rosanna it admitted that “key session content” from therapeutic discussions was automatically uploaded. It also told her: “Very private material can be shared in the context of treatment.”.
In September Rosanna attempted to clarify exactly what had been shared on her medical notes by submitting a subject access request to SLaM. So far SLaM has failed to respond to that request.
She is concerned that sharing therapy notes, including those of children, could present a danger to patients.

She said: “Where trauma is involved, it can create a safety risk. You don’t want the most intimate parts of your life getting into the hands of the wrong person. SLaM’s own list of what it shares includes all events from its child and adolescent mental health services.”
She added: “When I asked what was being shared, a senior therapist told me he didn’t know all the answers. SLaM now accepts staff and patients may not have been given enough information.”
Rosanna said there should have been a choice to opt out of such information being shared, but SLaM had failed to inform her that her therapy notes would be available to tens of thousands of staff.

Her MP, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, asked the government what guidance had been issued to mental health trusts on sharing therapy notes. James Frith, a junior health minister, replied that all records “relating to direct care are shared on a basis of implied consent”.

Rosanna said: “It’s implicit that therapy is confidential unless you’re told otherwise, within the normal safeguarding limits. Patients should be told where their data is going. You can’t object to something if you don’t know it’s happening and you haven’t been told.

“I paused my psychotherapy because I couldn’t be confident where what I said in treatment would end up. I’ve been without mental health secondary care support since, including while a parent was seriously ill and after they died.
“I am concerned other people receiving therapy from SLaM will see this and, like me, pause treatment. I would urge you not to, and to learn about your data rights instead.”

Rosanna supports the new planned single patient record, but thinks the focus should be on sharing medical details, not the contents of therapy sessions. “Transparency over what will be on the shared record and the option to opt out is essential,” she said.
Prof Derek Tracy, SLaM’s chief medical officer executive, said: “We apologise again to the patient for the delays in responding to her concerns.

“We put the utmost importance on patient confidentiality and the trust placed in us by our patients and service users. We have clear guidance on limiting the information recorded. This includes any significant changes or themes, risks and agreed actions.

“Clinicians also have the option to limit access to information to local teams in the trust without it being shared more widely and mask parts of the record as appropriate to balance sharing relevant information and respect privacy.”

Andy Bell, the chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, said: “Normally when you start therapy there’s a discussion about confidentiality. The therapist will say ‘If you tell me something that creates a safeguarding risk to yourself or others I will have to tell x y and z’. Not everything can remain confidential.
“A situation like this does raise issues about the boundaries of what is shareable and what isn’t, and what is appropriate to go on someone’s notes and what absolutely shouldn’t.
“If a patient is finding out information about themselves on the system that they didn’t expect, that suggests that the system isn’t working properly.”

articles.title: AFP: US arms sale, military financing to boost PH defense posture, modernization
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday said the continued military assistance of the United States would help strengthen Manila's defense capabilities and support its modernization…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 12:58pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday said the continued military assistance of the United States would help strengthen Manila's defense capabilities and support its modernization efforts.

AFP spokesperson Colonel Francel Margareth Padilla issued the statement following the White House's announcement of approved foreign military financing (FMF) for the Philippines' critical defense capabilities worth over $2-billion. America will also provide $400 million in FMF for the Philippines' maritime defense in the South China Sea.
"We appreciate the continued support of the United States in strengthening the AFP's capabilities," Padilla said.
"These forms of assistance contribute to our ongoing modernization and efforts to develop a credible defense posture," she added.
The AFP's statement indicates a total US assistance package worth more than $5 billion, covering weapons sale and increased military financing.

For now, the AFP is prioritizing the procurement of kinetic capabilities and equipment to strengthen the country's territorial defense amid the presence of Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy vessels in Philippine waters.
In an ambush interview, AFP chief General Antonio Nafarrete said, "We concentrate now on kinetic, 'yung mga kinetic na requirement natin (those our kinetic requirements)."

"Basically for territorial defense talaga, ensuring that kapag may mga, kasi ito ano natin archipelagic, pumapasok na 'yung mga PLA na mga naval vessels dito sa sea lines of communications natin, that's international kasi so we must be able to have that deterrent capability para malaman nila na hindi basta-bastang ano rito."

(Basically for territorial defense, ensuring that when there are, because this is our archipelagic territory, PLA naval vessels enter our sea lines of communications, that's international, so we must be able to have that deterrent capability so they know it is not easy.)
Padilla stressed that any acquisition would undergo the appropriate assessment and procurement processes based on the AFP's operational requirements and national defense priorities.

Through the $400-million FMF, the AFP should be able to expand its operational reach and deterrence capabilities in the South China Sea, particularly in territorial waters that overlap with the West Philippine Sea.
The assistance is expected to cover long-range fires, command-and-control systems, critical infrastructure, and multi-domain drones.

Meanwhile, the White House said the Department of National Defense (DND) had agreed to a $37-million contract with a US firm for super intelligence-enabled mission support, and a $63-million initiative to modernize its defense cloud infrastructure for super intelligence applications. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon’s explanations of body disposal ‘ring hollow’, court hears
articles.summary:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies on Friday as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.
The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.
But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.

The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.
“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.
“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.
“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”

Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.
Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.
“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he said.

blocks.caption: Luke Davies and Jesse Baird.  Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.
after newsletter promotion
The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.
Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.
Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.
The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.

Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.
“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.

Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: NextDC vows to keep future datacentres away from homes after community backlash in Melbourne
articles.summary:
Public expectations around datacentres have changed in the age of AI, chief executive Craig Scroggie says

  • Get our

blocks.text: Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.

The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.
The share price has since recovered to over $9 a share, but not before rival Goodman Group bought a nearly 10% stake in the business.
Shareholders revolted against the company at the AGM, issuing a second strike against executive pay, but the resulting motion on whether to spill the board was resoundingly defeated on Friday.

The chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said it was his “hardest AGM” in 15 years, and that he ultimately took responsibility for “delivery, power, planning, approvals, construction and community support”.
“At M3, we needed to work more closely with our power and construction partners, and with the community,” he said. “We are now doing that.”
Scroggie said the community deserved to be heard earlier than they had been during the Jemena construction works, and it was NextDC’s job to do that.
“M3 has certainly changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours,” he said.

“For more than 15 years we’ve built datacentres right across the country, and what earned trust then is not enough now. Community expectations have moved in the age of artificial intelligence and we must move with them.”

In addition to a new community consultative committee, including a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders, NextDC has said it will have a dedicated project website and contact channels with defined response times for complaints and inquiries.
NextDC’s chair, Doug Flynn, also revealed that the company would change where it builds in future.
“Given community sensitivities, we do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties,” Flynn said.
“The pushback against datacentres is very different right now than it was … six or so years ago.”
Flynn said that the M3 site in inner Melbourne had been an industrial site for 100 years, and had petrochemical works on it before NextDC built the datacentre.
After the blowback to taller power poles led to a delayed expansion, Flynn said the Jemena employee overseeing community engagement left the business.
“They recognise that they were just charging ahead regardless of community,” he said. “And they got a bloody nose.
“Unfortunately, we did as well.”
A spokesperson for Jemena declined to comment, but pointed to a September statement announcing its general manager for electricity networks had decided to step down.

articles.title: White House replaces cyber security chief after tech outages
articles.summary: Sean Cairncross is leaving his role as national cyber director after a chaotic week of tech outages. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will assume the position in an acting…

image.caption: Kirsten A. Davies will take over as acting national cyber directorImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United Statesover the week led to disruptions in air travel, banking and national security systems.

Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
Cairncross leaves after US tech outages

The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.

During Trump's first stint in the Oval Office, Cairncross took on various roles as a White House insider. He was ⁠also an executive at ​the Republican National Committee before becoming the cybersecurity chief.
