articles.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
articles.summary: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.

blocks.text: The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.

Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.

Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"

According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,

Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

articles.title: Cale88 classified as MSME --DTI witness
articles.summary: Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband Manases Carpio, is classified as a Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME), a defense witness said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 12:00pm
Cale88 Foods Corporation which is being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio, is classified as a Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME), a defense witness said Friday.

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo for Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group made the testimony during Day 45 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Duterte.
“Ito po (Cale88) ay MSME po kasi siya dahil po dung po sa project cost niya, below 15 million pesos,” Rodolfo, who also serves as the Managing Head of the Board of Investments, said.
(Cale88 is MSME because the project cost is below P15 million.)
Rodolfo then said Cale88 applied for a Certificate of Registration of an Export Enterprise before the BOI Extension in Davao and secured subsequent approval from the same office.

“We streamlined the BOI system in 2016 for MSMEs under a Board Resolution, meaning the evaluation and approval [of a business] is now delegated function. This means that is the business is in Luzon, it would be under the Executive Director of Industry Development Service. Outside Luzon, it will depend on the jurisdiction of BOI Extension Office. Para dito po [sa Cale88], BOI Extension Office sa Davao ‘yung nag evaluate at nag approve,” Rodolfo pointed out.
(It is the BOI Davao office which evaluated and approved its application.)

“Dahil po sa na-register po siya, ina-assume ko lang po na wala po nakuhang objection ‘yung Davao office po natin [sa Cale88 application for Certificate of Registration of an Export Enterprise]. Wala po akong nakita dun sa kanilang evaluation report na merong nag-object,” he added.
(Since it was registered, I assume that nobody objected to its application, and that our Davao office did not find any things objectionable to its application based on the evaluation report.)
Rodolfo also said that as an MSME, Cale88 is not required to publish Certificate of Registration of an Export Enterprise in newspaper for general circulation.

“This requirement does not apply to Cale88 being an MSME. What we do is we post the notice [of its Certificate of Registration of an Export Enterprise] on our BOI website kasi medyo mahal rin po mag-publish sa newspaper of general circulation,” Rodolfo said.

Defense team lawyer Justin Gular said Rodolfo’s testimony disputes the findings of prosecution witness and financial forensic expert Alex Cabrera who earlier testified that Cale88 is not a real functioning business based on Cabrera’s analysis of the financial records of the Vice President and her husband.

“The exact term, Your Honor, if I may, by the supposed forensic expert is that Cale88 is allegedly an implausible business model. And of course, we seek to dispute, among other things, that monies were received by Mans Carpio from this corporation,” Gular said.

Cabrera, an accountant-lawyer, earlier testified that the Vice President and her husband have unexplained wealth worth P817 million to P1.5 billion due to non-declaration of their assets in their joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), including income from Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Defense witness and AML Consulting PH head, Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente, testified a day ago that there were red flags in Cale88 Foods Corporation operations given that the firm only has two employees, received P319 million remittances from China and recorded 757 covered transactions and suspicious transactions worth P1.2 billion.
Dela Fuente, however, said such red flags are not automatically illegal. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: NBI finds that samples from Cavite crematorium were not pet ashes
articles.summary: Five pet owners are seeking justice after forensic tests showed that samples given to them as cremated ashes of their pets were not animal remains, the Philippine Animal Welfare Society said.

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 11:49am
Representatives from Philippine Animal Welfare Society accompany five pet owners as they seek accountability over the alleged improper disposal of their pets' remains by a Cavite pet cremato
PAWS via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Five pet owners are seeking justice after forensic tests showed that samples given to them as cremated ashes of their pets were not animal remains, the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) said.

In a Facebook post on Thursday, November 19, the animal rights group said it accompanied the five complainants in seeking accountability over the alleged improper disposal of their deceased pets entrusted to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium.
The case came after dumped animal remains were discovered in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, by Luna and Furry Friends.

The five complainants said in their sworn statements that they paid a combined P44,400 for cremation and related services, expecting that their pets would be properly cremated and their ashes returned to them.
The complainants, who are seeking justice for Harley, Chichay, Crunch, Jennifer and Sweet, took their oaths before Assistant State Prosecutor Evee Eunice De Keyser as part of the proceedings.
PAWS said the complaint cited forensic examination by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), which found that the tested samples were not consistent with genuine cremated animal remains.

Laboratory analysis detected silicon, iron, potassium and aluminum in the samples. NBI forensic chemists said their composition was inconsistent with that of cremated animal remains, according to PAWS.
Criminal complaints have been filed against Jonathan Galaura Legaspi, Jeffrey Cuartero Haylar, Jenina Malonzo Haylar and Reinier Roqueño Peñaflor, alias "Benok."
The complaints include estafa against Legaspi and alleged violations of Republic Act 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, against all four respondents, PAWS said.
The group said it stands with the families in seeking justice and accountability.
"Every pet deserves dignity and respect and every grieving family deserves the truth," PAWS said.
PAWS also urged other clients of the crematorium who may have been affected to keep their urns, receipts, transaction records and other relevant evidence.
They were advised to coordinate with the NBI Environmental Crime Division regarding the filing of complaints and the proper submission of samples for examination.

articles.title: Trump administration moves to drop lawsuit challenging Alaska Senate election result
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a…

image.caption: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola was declared the winner of the state's Senate race Tuesday. Two days later, the Trump administration moved to get its lawsuit blocking the victory from being certified dismissed. (Kerry Tasker/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.
Lawsuit demanded Democrat Mary Peltola's win not be certified until probe could prove voters weren't confused

The legal challenge focused on the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court had already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy was legal and that he could be on the ballot.

Alaska's state government, currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.

In their filing, U.S. Justice Department (DOJ) attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground."

That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by candidate Dan J. Sullivan.
Trump slams Democrats for Alaska's double Dan Sullivan drama

The DOJ filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump's direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.

The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement.

items: Dirty tricks or much ado about nothing? Why Alaska, for once, is front and centre in midterms

blocks.text: Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before election day. articles.title: Texas death row execution takes more than an hour as inmate heard complaining of pain
articles.summary: The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative…

image.caption: This image provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows Reinaldo Dennes on April 14. He was executed Thursday in a procedure that took 63 minutes to complete. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital. He was the second person put to death in the country Thursday after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
Reinaldo Dennes yelled out 'I don't think this is normal,' before dying 63 minutes after being strapped down

The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.
He was the second person put to death in the country Thursday after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population. They also follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father."
Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"

Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."

Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."
Pentagon’s plan to livestream execution sparks outrage
Procedures followed appropriately, say prison officials

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.
She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used are in accordance with the state's procedures.
This image provided by the Florida Department of Corrections shows Thomas Mitchell Overton, who was put to death in Florida Thursday. (Florida Department of Corrections/The Associated Press)

Earlier in the day, Florida carried out its execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."
Florida has carried out half of all U.S. executions in 2026

Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. The executions follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who've waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. After a record-setting Thursday, Florida is planning two more executions in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has taken an aggressive stance on death row executions since taking office. (Chris O'Meara/The Associated Press)
Overton case
In Florida, Overton was seen strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.
"I've never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone," Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors' home or gated community. "I didn't kill the MacIvors."

The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared the inmate dead.

The MacIvors' bodies were found in their Tavernier, Fla., home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state's database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors' home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors' home.
Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.
Michael MacIvor's sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man's sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.

"One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive," Sharon MacIvor said. "Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him."
Christa Pike's lawyers demand answers, transparency over botched execution
Dennes case

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building's back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting. Records showed she also distracted the security guard at Dennes' request.
The guard was shot twice but recovered and identified Dennes as his assailant.

Police found the jeweller's body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 US in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.
Dennes's attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

articles.title: Who is DTI exec Ceferino Rodolfo?
articles.summary: Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo of DTI"s Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group took the witness stand on Friday, November 20, for the 45th day of…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 11:29am

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo of DTI’s Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group took the witness stand on Friday, November 20, for the 45th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Rodolfo, who also serves as the Managing Head of the Board of Investments, has been with the DTI since March 2013 when he was appointed Assistant Secretary.
Rodolfo was promoted to DTI Undersecretary in February 2016, a position he has held since.
Rodolfo will testify on business registration Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of the Vice President.

The defense team is offering Rodolfo’s testimony to prove that Cale88 Foods Corporation is a duly registered export enterprise with the BOI and is engaged in the lawful and legitimate business of producing and exporting Banana Chips.
Likewise, Rodolfo will testify that Cale88 Foods Corporation is a duly registered Export Enterprise with the Board of Investments and is legally entitled to the following incentives:

items: Income Tax Holiday
Special Corporate Income Tax
Duty Exemption and
VAT Exemption and Zero Rating.

blocks.text: Rodolfo’s testimony is also being offered to prove that he issued Cale88 Foods Corporation's Certificate of Registration No. 2021-186 as an Export Enterprise engaged in PSIC 10309 Manufacture of Foods Products, Export of Producer of Banana Chips.

Prosecution witness and financial forensic expert Alex Cabrera, an accountant-lawyer, earlier testified that the Vice President and her husband have unexplained wealth worth P817 million to P1.5 billion due to non-declaration of their assets in their joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), including income from Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Defense witness and AML Consulting PH head, Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente, earlier testified that there were red flags in Cale88 Foods Corporation operations given that the firm only has two employees, received P319 million remittances from China and recorded 757 covered transactions and suspicious transactions worth P1.2 billion.
Dela Fuente, however, said such red flags are not automatically illegal. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Senate impeachment court summons Sara Duterte's spox over remarks on senator-judges
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court issued a show-cause order against Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over his remarks to reporters about the credibility of the…

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 11:17am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court issued a show-cause order against Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over his remarks to reporters about the credibility of the senator-judges.
Sen. Erwin Tulfo raised the show-cause order on Friday, November 20, saying Panelo was discrediting the senator-judges.
“He's not party to this case pero siya po ang tagapagsalita ng vice presidente. Tama po ba 'yun? I mean, I believe parang meron hong problema rito,” Tulfo said.
(He is not a party to this case, yet he acts as the vice president's spokesperson. Is that right? I mean, I believe there seems to be a problem here.)

“I mean, you are the spokesperson of the vice president na on trial here and then magko-komento ka hinggil sa mga senator-judges of the impeachment court eh para namang wala pong respeto sa ika nga impeachment court,” he added.

(I mean, you are the spokesperson of the Vice President who is on trial here, and then you comment on the senator-judges of the impeachment court—it seems disrespectful to the impeachment court, so to speak.)
Senate presiding officer Francis Escudero then ordered the Clerk of Court to issue a show-cause order against Panelo.
On November 20, Panelo told reporters that some senator-judges had acted like the prosecution.
He was referring to the line of questioning by the senator-judges directed at defense witness and lawyer Rainer dela Fuente.
“Ang napansin po natin, ang nagta-try na magbasag ng credibility niya ay yung senator-judges natin. Sa punto pa lang na iyon, I think that is improper,” Panelo said, according to media reports.
(What we have noticed is that those trying to destroy his/her credibility are our senator-judges. On that point alone, I think that is improper.)
“Hindi po trabaho ng senator-judge 'yan; ang dapat po na gumagawa niyan ay ang prosecution,” he added.
(That is not the job of a senator-judge; the prosecution is the one who should be doing that.)

articles.title: Fiona the hippo dies after ingesting knitted hat at Cincinnati zoo
articles.summary:
Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail

Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after…

blocks.text: Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media.
With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.

The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.

“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo statement said.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press.

Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying to push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines.

“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo had said on social media. Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
Within an hour of the announcement, visitors began leaving flowers and cards by a hippo statue outside the zoo. “Forever our Fiona,” one note read.
Fiona became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own.

Fiona was born six weeks premature at just 29lb (13.2kgs), falling below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. Because she was initially too weak to nurse, Cincinnati Zoo staff hand-milked her mother while documenting Fiona’s recovery through photos and videos that captivated the internet.

Fiona admirers flocked to the zoo when her death was announced. Amy Haacke, a special educator from Dayton, said outside the Cincinnati Zoo that she has been a “huge fan” of Fiona since she was born because she likes underdogs. Haacke said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom and owns three Fiona shirts.
“We were coming here anyway, but it kind of means a lot to be here,” Haacke said on Thursday. “We were here when she was first born and, I guess, now we’re here when she’s gone.”

Aftab Pureval, the Cincinnati mayor, said on social media that Fiona was “a symbol of perseverance and joy” in the city. Mike DeWine, the governor of Ohio, called her “a true icon”. The Cincinnati Bengals also expressed condolences, dubbing Fiona “the queen of the Queen City”.
The Cincinnati Reds baseball team also paid tribute: “Forever an icon. Rest in peace, Fiona.”
Chelsea Clinton, daughter of Hilary and Bill Clinton, shared her memories of Fiona and a tribute. “I will always treasure the art Fiona made for me and the smiles she gave me,” Clinton wrote.

The San Antonio zoo – whose hippo, Timothy, had a long-distance romance with Fiona – offered heartfelt condolences to the Cincinnati zoo. “Fiona held a special place in our San Antonio Zoo family and community … beyond the playful romance, Timothy and Fiona’s connection created a unique opportunity to educate audiences,” the zoo wrote. “Fiona’s impact reached far beyond Cincinnati, and the joy she brought to so many will never be forgotten.”

In a joint post with JD Vance, the US vice-president, on Instagram, second lady Usha Vance shared a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through a glass wall of her enclosure. The family has a home in Cincinnati.
“We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona,” she said in the caption. “Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo.”

Her survival in 2017 had offered a much-needed positive chapter for the zoo following months of intense public backlash over the fatal shooting of Harambe, the silverback gorilla killed after a child breached his enclosure.

Wildlife facilities have long warned of the dangers posed by foreign objects dropped or blown into animal habitats. Past incidents have demonstrated the fatal risks involved, including a rare antelope that choked to death on a plastic cap of a snack pouch at a Tennessee zoo two years ago, and a polar bear at a German zoo that died in 2014 after swallowing a visitor’s dropped jacket.

articles.title: Paolo Panelo issued show cause order by Senate impeachment court
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Friday issued a show cause order against Vice President Sara Duterte's spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over his comments regarding the alleged partiality of several…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 10:49am

The Senate impeachment court on Friday issued a show cause order against Vice President Sara Duterte's spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over his comments regarding the alleged partiality of several senator-judges.

Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo raised concerns about Panelo's statements on Day 45 of Duterte's impeachment trial, asking Senate impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero if there was something the court could do about it.
Panelo had asserted that some senator-judges were acting as prosecutors.

Tulfo said, "He's not party to this case pero siya po ang tagapagsalita ng bise presidente. Tama po ba 'yun? I believe parang mayroong problema dito. I mean, you are the spokesperson of the vice president, na on trial here, and then magkokomento ko hinggil sa senator-judges of the impeachment court."

(He's not party to this case but he's the spokesperson of the vice president. Is that proper? I believe there seems to be a problem here. I mean, you are the spokesperson of the vice president who is on trial here, and then you make comments about the senator-judges of the impeachment court.)

Escudero replied by saying that Panelo was not a lawyer nor witness in the trial, so he was not covered by the sub judice ruling. However, Escudero said that with the suppletory application of the Rules of Court, specifically Rule 71 on the Rules of Contempt, Panelo is susceptible to any orders by the court in relation to speech or action about the court.
"If I understand the motion, instead of asking him to explain, it will be in the form of a show cause order, Honorable Senator-judge Erwin. Is that your pleasure, sir?" Escudero said.
"Yes, Mister Presiding Officer. That's my point, sir… I will therefore file a motion to issue a show cause order for the spokesperson of the vice president," Tulfo said.
With no one objecting to the motion, Escudero directed the Clerk of Court to issue the show cause order.
GMA News Online has requested comment from Panelo regarding the matter, but he has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sean Cairncross out, Kirsten A. Davies in as White House national cyber director: source
articles.summary: Sean Cairncross is out as the White House's national cyber director, a source close to the White House told CBC News on Thursday.

image.caption: Sean Cairncross, seen attending a conference in Menlo Park, Calif., earlier this week, is out as the White House national cyber director. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Sean Cairncross is out as the White House's national cyber director, a source close to the White House told CBC News on Thursday.
Shake-up follows recent series of high-profile tech problems state-side
He's being replaced, in an acting capacity, by Kirsten A. Davies, who has been serving as the chief information officer at the U.S. Department of War.
CBC News is not identifying the source, who provided the information on condition they not be named.

The shake-up follows a series of high-profile tech problems state-side in recent days — including an apparent IT incident that caused a nation-wide ground stop of flights in the U.S. last week, and headline-grabbing service outages involving Microsoft products and bank transactions. The U.S. National Security Agency also saw its classified internal communications go offline.
The national cyber director leads the Office of the National Cyber Director, which was created in 2021.
U.S. President Donald Trump is said to be supportive of the change, which the administration views as strengthening its cybersecurity team.

An existing biography for Davies on the Department of War's website cites her near two decades of prior "executive leadership experience at the intersection of cybersecurity, enterprise technology, and large-scale organizational transformation," before joining the government.

Cairncross was confirmed by the U.S. Senate for the role in August 2025. A White House statement at that time had touted his "extensive leadership experience," prior to taking the cyber director role.

articles.title: Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win
articles.summary:
President had sought to block results if Democrat won race that featured two candidates named Dan Sullivan

In a legal filing on Thursday, the Trump administration

blocks.text: In a legal filing on Thursday, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the midterm elections seeking to block the certification of the US Senate race in Alaska should Democrat Mary Peltola win.

The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska supreme court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was legal and that he could be on the ballot.

Peltola did win the election, with 50.13% of the vote, giving her more than the combined vote totals of all other candidates, including the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, and a second Daniel Sullivan, who was reportedly recruited to enter the race by Democrats to siphon votes away from the sitting senator.

The suit was filed at the direction of Donald Trump saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.
The administration moved on Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.
Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit the “decoy” Dan Sullivan.
Peltola denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join the Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.

The legal filing came a day after Alaska concluded its vote-count and used ranked-choice tabulation to decide races where no candidate got more then 50% of the votes cast, including the election for the state’s sole representative in Congress.

One of those candidates, Eric Hafner, was apparently also included on the ballot in an attempt to confuse voters. Hafner, who was allowed to contest the race as a Democrat, over the objections of the state’s Democratic party, and despite having no connection to the state and currently being incarcerated in federal prison in New York, got 22,715 votes.
Had all of his ballots been cast for Hill, who was backed by the state’s Democratic party, Hill would have defeated Begich.

articles.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
articles.summary: The scheme is expected to be approved at Friday's UK-EU summit, with new deals on food trade and carbon emissions also on the table.

blocks.text: Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

articles.title: US army postpones plan to detonate bomb-making chemical amid outcry
articles.summary:
The controlled detonation can lead to a plume containing lead particles, worrying residents and state officials

The US army has

blocks.text: The US army has delayed its plan to detonate a stash of bomb-making chemicals in south-eastern Iowa as questions swirl about the public health risks.
The army was set to blow up about 5 tons of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, at noon on Friday, a move it described as the safest way to dispose of the highly sensitive compound.
During the controlled explosion, barrels of the material would be stored inside concrete structures and surrounded by sand-filled Hesco barriers reaching up two stories high.

Army officials advised certain residents of Middletown to evacuate between 8am and 2pm local time, due to the potential for window damage. The vibrations from the two blasts would not last long but could break old windows in town, and the resulting dust was expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
The detonation is also expected to produce a plume containing lead particles.

Officials have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north. Updated maps showed the plume’s shift, and the army will continue to update the map based on weather. Some schools in the path of the plume have already canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the path of the plume.
While the army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after the detonation, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
Iowa’s top leaders appeared to learn about the plan along with the public. The office of the Iowa governor, Kim Reynolds, was first briefed on Monday about the public advisory, her office said.

“An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation,” governor-elect Rob Sand wrote on X on Thursday. “The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse.”
Adam Telle, the acting secretary of the US army, alluded to the criticism in his Thursday announcement about the delayed detonation.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” he wrote on X, adding that he was engaging state officials.
The plan is now expected to proceed on Monday. According to Telle, it’s the “latest possible moment”, before temperatures drop, which could risk destabilizing the material.

Middletown residents learned in March that the army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.

“The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt Col Daniel Nosse, the commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.

The army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on 13 November approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday’s detonation.

That permit required the army to track specific rates of potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday’s original advisory to communities as far as 100 miles (160km) away.

Just a few miles north-west, the Danville community school district will close on Friday, the superintendent said in an announcement on Tuesday. Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but there were enough uncertainties that made canceling “the most responsible decision”.
“I am not suggesting that the detonation will result in unsafe conditions,” he wrote. “The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon.”

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles (32km) north-east of the ammunition plant, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure on Sunday, when the initial map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area. Schools and the public library will close on Friday and the local fire department planned to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.
The city of nearly 2,000 residents was no longer in the plume in an updated map.

“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” the deputy city clerk, Amy Stucker, said on Wednesday. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s department of occupational and environmental health, said it was encouraging to see that the army and the EPA were doing all they could to minimize the dust, but it was still unknown how much would end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.

Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' faked kidnapping, created video for sympathy, defence says
articles.summary: A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain sympathy from his investors, who were trying to recover funds from him.
Lawyer for alleged kidnapper says Aiden Pleterski faked video so his investors would see it, have sympathy
'Crypto King' faked kidnapping, defence says

A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski's alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain sympathy from his investors.
Pleterski denied both assertions while being cross-examined Thursday during the Toronto trial for three of his alleged kidnappers in Ontario Superior Court.

The video, which was played for the jury earlier in the trial and was previously obtained by CBC News, shows a beaten Pleterski apologizing to his investors and explaining what happened to their money.
Defence lawyer Leora Shemesh suggested Pleterski made the video himself to go viral and be seen by his investors, who were trying to recover their lost funds through a bankruptcy proceeding.
"This is an apology that's going to your very angry investors, who were going to see you with two black eyes and take pity and sympathy with you," she said.

items: Secretly recorded videos of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski meeting alleged kidnapper played at trial
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping

blocks.text: Shemesh is representing Alfredo Paladino who is charged — alongside Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry — with kidnapping and extorting Pleterski.
Pleterski previously testified that he was beaten, tortured and thought he was going to die during the three-day ordeal in early December 2022.

From left, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting the so-called 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, atlanticmastoronto/Instagram)

The Crown is alleging Heywood was the "driving force" behind the kidnapping and lost money investing with Pleterski, while Paladino and Henry carried out the kidnapping. Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearm and assault offences. All three men have pleaded not guilty.

Pleterski, who turned 28 on Wednesday, was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf. Instead, he spent much of it on his lifestyle. He has yet to be sentenced.
Pleterski questioned about kidnapping video
Pleterski testified Thursday that his kidnappers recorded the video while he was being held in a basement and instructed him on what to say.
"They told me to take all the blame for absolutely everything," he said.

Shemesh went through the transcript of the video line-by-line and questioned Pleterski about why he was including specific personal details such as how he was charged with assaulting his girlfriend in Florida and the year he began investing with his own money.
"During a kidnapping you told them that?" Shemesh pointedly asked him.
Pleterski said he was instructed to explain his story from the beginning and a lot of information, including the incident involving his girlfriend, was public at the time.
Defence lawyer Leora Shemesh, seen at right in this courtroom sketch, is representing Alfredo Paladino, right, in the trial involving the alleged kidnapping of Pleterski. (Pam Davies/CBC)

He testified that some of what he said in the nearly 14-minute video was true, some information was false — he said he was forced to say it by his kidnappers — and some he just said himself without instruction.

In the video, Pleterski details assets he "dispersed" to his former landlord Sandeep Gupta before his bankruptcy proceeding began, including luxury vehicles and at least two Rolex watches and a Jacob & Co. watch that he testified he bought for more than $300,000.

items: Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping

blocks.text: Pleterski testified Gupta wasn't actually hiding assets. He said he only told the kidnappers that so he could be released to set up a meeting with Gupta in hopes he would realize Pleterski was in trouble and alert the police.
Pleterski testified that he sold the Jacob & Co. watch and said he believed he got cash for it, but didn't remember who he sold it to or when, nor how he received the cash.
"Sandeep Gupta had your cars, Sandeep Gupta had your jewelry and Sandeep Gupta was holding money for you," Shemesh said.
Gupta testified earlier in the trial and denied hiding any assets for Pleterski.
Pleterski partied at rapper Drake's home

Heywood's defence lawyer, Hussein Aly, finished his cross-examination of Pleterski Thursday afternoon after two days of continually accusing Pleterski of lying, both while running a fraudulent investment scheme and during his testimony in the kidnapping trial.

Pleterski testified that Heywood invested with him then began threatening him about getting his money back. Pleterski said he was afraid after receiving threats from many people, including Heywood, so he hired security.
Aly questioned Pleterski about why he would hire a security company that belonged to Heywood's friend if Pleterski was being threatened by Heywood.

Akil Heywood's lawyer Hussein Aly showed the jury this photo of a group including Akil Heywood wearing a hat standing next to rapper Drake and the security guard wearing a blue shirt. Champagnepapi is Drake's instagram handle. (Akil Heywood/Facebook)
The jury heard the company is owned by Drake's security guard and Aly showed them photos of Heywood, Drake and the security guard together.
"You saw these photos on Akil Heywood's Instagram," Aly said to Pleterski.
Pleterski responded that he doesn't remember seeing them.
Aly also questioned why Pleterski went to a party at Drake's house in the spring of 2022 if he knew that Heywood was friends with the rapper.

Pleterski said he didn't know Heywood was going to be there, but said Heywood asked him for his money while at Drake's house, and that the security guard noticed the conversation, approached them, then put his hand on Heywood's shoulder and said "not here."

items: 'Crypto King' or 'Lying King'? Aiden Pleterski says he was neither at alleged kidnappers' trial

blocks.text: Aly has suggested Pleterski made up Heywood's involvement in the alleged kidnapping because he was mad about Heywood and another investor forcing Pleterski into bankruptcy.
"I could ask you questions for 100 days," Aly said to Pleterski. "You're never going to admit that you're lying about Akil Heywood's involvement in what happened to you."
Cross examination of Pleterski is expected to continue tomorrow afternoon.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Angelina King is a reporter with CBC Toronto's enterprise unit where she investigates a wide range of topics. She has a particular interest in crime, justice issues and human interest stories. Angelina started her career in her home city of Saskatoon where she spent much of her time covering the courts. You can contact her at angelina.king@cbc.ca or @angelinaaking

blocks.text: Fiona the hippo has died at the Cincinnati Zoo in the US after swallowing a visitor's hat which was accidentally thrown into her enclosure. She was nine years old.

"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," the zoo said. "The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."
Fiona was born in 2017 prematurely, with the hippo becoming a social media sensation. At the time of her birth, she only weighed 29 pounds (13 kilograms) and was in a fight to survive.

articles.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.

blocks.text: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

The company says a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the waters of the Skeena River Tuesday, with diesel from the locomotive then leaking more than a kilometre downstream. It's the second such incident this year, following a similar derailment during extreme weather this past March.
Company is cleaning up 2nd diesel spill into Skeena River this year following suspected rockslide

The debate over shipping hazardous materials by rail has been reignited after a CN Rail train came off the tracks in northwest B.C., leaking diesel into the salmon-bearing Skeena River for the second time in eight months.

The company says a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the water Tuesday, with diesel from the locomotive then leaking more than a kilometre downstream.
It's the second such incident this year, following a similar derailment during extreme weather this past March.

In an update Thursday morning, CN Rail said it had repaired the track and traffic is running again, and the B.C. government says a containment boom and absorbent pads are in place and a surface water sampling plan has been drafted.
The province also says it's asked CN Rail to provide an estimate for how much diesel was spilled, but so far, the volume has not been shared.
Drone footage from the site shows a visible sheen traveling downstream.
Former NDP MP Taylor Bachrach, who lives in the region and previously served as the party's transport critic, called the derailments a "wake-up call."
"The railroad, for hundreds of kilometres in our region, goes right next to the Skeena River," he said, identifying it as highly important for salmon.
"When we're talking about the shipment of dangerous goods along that rail line, the implications, the consequences of a major disaster are really unthinkable."

The debate over rail shipments is especially fraught in northwest B.C., where the Port of Prince Rupert has emerged as key to shipping energy products to overseas Asian markets in light of the U.S.-Canada trade war.
What politicians get wrong about the B.C. oil tanker ban
Even so, efforts to build a pipeline to transport heavy crude oil to the North Coast have been resisted due to concerns about environmental impacts.
Likewise, proposals like that from Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil to Prince Rupert a day have also met with opposition.
They are made more challenging by the Liberal government's support of the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, which blocks large oil tankers from travelling along B.C.'s northern coast.
Concerns over response time
No major spill incidents were recorded between Terrace and Prince Rupert in the decade prior to this year, according to provincial data.
Even so, the more recent spills have First Nations in the area worried about the increased train traffic through the sensitive region.
CN Rail says cleanup efforts are underway after a train derailed into the Skeena River on Nov. 17, 2026. (Submitted by Carl J. Reibin)
Kitsumkalum First Nation Chief Councillor Troy Sam said he wants to make sure the province and industry groups work with First Nations to improve response times.
"My position is to make sure this doesn't happen again," he said. "What did we learn from this incident and how could we respond better?"

Gitxsan Hereditary Chief Skogam'Lahkx Toby Howard said his government is calling for all cargo train traffic between Burns Lake and Prince Rupert to be put on hold until the full track can be inspected for safety.
"The whole system ... it's pretty old," he said. "There are a lot of things we need to address."
Diesel leaking into Skeena River after train derails near Terrace, B.C.

Peter Ross, an environmental toxicologist with the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, said that while diesel tends to dissipate and evaporate on its own, it still poses a risk to fish and wildlife who come into contact with it.
And, he said, the two spills within a few months raise larger concerns.
"I think this really speaks to the dangers of transport when it comes to petrochemicals," he said.

items: 2 hospitalized after CN Rail train derails into Skeena River near Terrace, B.C.
Gitxsan hereditary chiefs call for halt to rail cargo as diesel leaks from train derailment along Skeena River

blocks.text: While he was confident officials would manage the spill, Ross wondered whether they would see the bigger picture.
"It's something we do very poorly as a society, is add all of these cumulative effects together to try to define the risk to fish and wildlife," he said.
With files from Catherine Garrett and Jason Peters

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 8:30am
Former Commission on Audit chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba.
Commission on Audit website
MANILA, Philippines — Former Commission on Audit chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba has taken his oath as an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court.
Cordoba took his oath before Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on Thursday, November 19.
He replaces Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, who reached compulsory retirement on November 16.
Before his appointment to the high court, he served as COA Chairperson from 2022to 2026.

Before that, he held several key positions in the Office of the President, which include appointments secretary with the rank of undersecretary from 2006 to 2007, undersecretary from 2003 to 2006, assistant executive secretary from 2002 to 2003, and technical assistant with the rank of Director IV from 2001 to 2002.
He also served as director of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. from 2008 to 2009.
Cordoba is the third justice of the Supreme Court to be appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
