articles.title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
articles.summary: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.

blocks.text: As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.
While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.
"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.
"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.
At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".

One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.
His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.

Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign., external The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75%, external, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.
Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.
The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.

The project is billed as "off-grid", external, relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment, external, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.

The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June , externalthat he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".

In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.

Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.
"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.
Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.
He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.
Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.

"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press, external, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.
This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.
There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.
On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre, external that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.
But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.

"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.
"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.
So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.

The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.
Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".
In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.
Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.
"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.

Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.

If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.

MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta,, external over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.

But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.
"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."

articles.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
articles.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.

blocks.text: Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty Images
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say
ByOrla Guerin
Senior international correspondentReporting fromIstanbul
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

blocks.text: Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

blocks.caption: Four-panel map series showing the expansion of Houthi-controlled territory in western and southern Yemen between August and November 2026. Houthi-held areas are shaded pink. Top left (August 2026): Houthi forces control much of western Yemen, including Sanaa, and launch an offensive south along t…

blocks.text: An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

blocks.caption: 3D satellite graphic showing Houthi-controlled territory (red) and contested areas (purple) around the government-controlled city of Taiz, southern Yemen, as of 18 November 2026

blocks.text: What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling

blocks.text: Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months

blocks.text: Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

articles.title: U.S. sanctions Canadian branch of Italian criminal organization, including funeral homes in Toronto area
articles.summary: The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, an Italian Mafia group.

image.caption: The Vescio Funeral Home in Maple, Ont., is pictured in an undated handout image. (U.S. Treasury)

blocks.text: Canada·New
The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, an Italian Mafia group.
One of six prominent gang members serves as president of funeral homes in Woodbridge, Maple and Toronto
The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, one of Italy's most powerful criminal organizations.

A statement from the U.S. Treasury said the enforcement targeted "a powerful transnational faction of the 'Ndrangheta" group in the Toronto area. That group has been involved in "drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, and other crimes," officials said.
The new sanctions target six people officials identified as key figures of the gang in the Toronto area, as well as the wife and children of one leader: Luigi Vescio Sr., 55.
Vescio Sr., who the statement says is known as "The Undertaker," serves as president of several funeral homes in Ontario, including:

items: Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Woodbridge, Ont.
Vescio Funeral Home (Maple) Inc. in Maple, Ont.
Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Toronto.

blocks.text: Described as a senior, Canadian-born member of the 'Ndrangheta, Vescio Sr. also controls a Toronto-based luxury limousine rental business: Phantom Limousine Services Inc. The businesses have now been sanctioned, as have members of his family.

His wife, Rose Vescio, and his two children, Luigi Vescio Jr. and Laura Vescio, were listed "for their roles in owning and operating the Vescio Funeral Homes" on Vescio Sr.'s behalf, the statement said.

items: Canada's deportation of alleged Mafia boss hinges on foreign eavesdropping
The Mafia from the mountains: Fighting Italy's most ruthless and secretive clans

blocks.text: Experts on the 'Ndrangheta have described the criminal syndicate as one of the most financially sophisticated in the West, with capital heavily invested in the world of finance and clan branches firmly ensconced around the globe, including in the Toronto and Montreal areas. Experts estimated the clans' annual income in 2021 would range from $50 billion to $85 billion a year.

The sanctions effectively cut off the people and businesses from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
The sanctions also targeted the Comancheros, one of the oldest biker gangs in Australia, also accused of running global drug trafficking operations.

articles.title: Letting Russia redraw Ukraine’s borders could set precedent for South China Sea — Slovenia
articles.summary: Allowing Russia to redraw Ukraine’s borders by force would weaken respect for international law far beyond Europe and could set a precedent for the South China Sea, Slovenian Foreign Minister…

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 7:30am

MANILA, Philippines — Allowing Russia to redraw Ukraine’s borders by force would weaken respect for international law far beyond Europe and could set a precedent for the South China Sea, Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer said.

Speaking to Philstar.com in Manila, where he attended the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, Kajzer said any successful attempt by Moscow in "changing borders" would carry over to disputes in Asia.

“If the international community would allow one country, a strong country in this particular case, basically to change the borders, or to violate international law with force, that would be kind of undermining the trust ... even including the South China Sea,” the Slovenian foreign minister said in an interview Friday, November 13. “Then somebody would say, ‘Okay, it was possible to do it there, why not here?’”

Kajzer said Russia’s war on Ukraine was “a clear violation of international law,” and noted it was carried out by a permanent member of the UN Security Council, “which is supposed to be the main guarantor of peace.”

"If this is going to be prolonged, this war of aggression, it's going to influence the deterioration of the situation here," he said, likening the state of the world to "a thunderstorm" that is embracing the whole planet," and adding that "all those wars are interconnected."

Slovenia in July was one of 14 governments, including the Philippines and the United States, that marked the 10th anniversary of the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award with a joint statement calling it final and binding on both Manila and Beijing.

The tribunal, which was set up under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, found no legal basis for China’s claim to “historic rights” inside its nine-dash line, which covers most of the resource-rich waters. China, which has refused to recognize the ruling, said in July the award was “a piece of waste paper” and lodged diplomatic protests with some of the countries that backed it.

During the ASEAN summit, Kajzer signed the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia for Slovenia, a decades-old pact that commits countries to agreeing to settle disputes peacefully. Slovakia and Cyprus signed the same day, bringing the number of signatories to 65.

The summit ended on November 17 without the long-delayed ASEAN–China code of conduct for the South China Sea, which Manila had aimed to conclude during its chairship this year. Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the two sides had provisionally agreed on about 80% of the draft.

Asked about Slovenia’s formal position on the South China Sea ruling, Kajzer said freedom of navigation is essential for maritime nations such as Slovenia and the Philippines, and for every other country, as 90% of global trade moves by sea.
"We have to respect international law, and it goes without saying that we Slovenes, we support international institutions, and in this particular case, UNCLOS should be respected," he said.

Kajzer was also asked what Slovenia’s own sea border dispute with Croatia could teach the Philippines. He said the two cases were not identical, but that “the law of the sea and international law ... should be respected."
"We have to insist on this, but of course, it also goes without saying that we should strive for good neighborhood relations," he said.

The dispute over Piran Bay, a small inlet in the northern Adriatic, goes back to the breakup of Yugoslavia. In 2017 an arbitral tribunal in The Hague awarded most of the bay to Slovenia. Croatia had withdrawn from the case two years earlier and has refused to implement the award.
Kajzer said arbitral awards “should be respected,” but suggested that governments “also try to find possibilities in this particular case to work with the neighbors.”

He said Slovenia and the Philippines could share their experience of such disputes, and added that he was “an optimistic person” who believed “it is always possible if you build a trustworthy relationship with your neighbor.”

Kajzer has taken a similar approach to Croatia since joining Prime Minister Janez Janša’s conservative government, which took office in June. At his first meeting with his Croatian counterpart, held in Dubrovnik, the two ministers agreed that outstanding bilateral issues should be handled “responsibly, pragmatically and gradually, based on mutual trust,” according to Slovenia’s foreign ministry.
Kajzer said the only solution to the world's wars is cooperation at the international level, and called the United Nations "the best instrument we have."
“We don’t have anything else at this moment,” he said. “I’m trying to keep the optimism, but the times are really, really demanding.”

Kajzer said he would invite Lazaro to Slovenia next year for the 22nd Bled Strategic Forum, the annual conference his ministry co-organizes. There he plans to propose a panel on relations between Central Europe and the Philippines, or ASEAN as a whole.

articles.title: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
articles.summary: Cumin-laced sodas are capturing a bigger market share in India as demand for homegrown flavours goes up.

blocks.text: It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.

Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.

Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.

There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.

According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.

"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."

Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.

But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.

Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.

"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

articles.title: 9-month-old dies of hypothermia in Gaza as territory heads into winter season
articles.summary: Kinan Arqiq was nine months old when he died of hypothermia in Gaza, as heavy rains caused flooding in makeshift tent cities.

image.caption: Ahmed Arqiq holds the body of his son, nine-month-old Kinan, the first death from hypothermia in Gaza this season. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New
Kinan Arqiq was nine months old when he died of hypothermia in Gaza, as heavy rains caused flooding in makeshift tent cities.
Ahmed Arqiq, 37, says his son Kinan froze to death overnight

Ahmed Arqiq walked through a crowd of mourners, carrying the lifeless body of his nine-month-old baby, Kinan, wrapped in a white blanket. With every laboured step he took, passersby gave him condolences. He quietly whispered prayers over his son’s body.
The prior morning at 4 a.m., the 37-year-old said he rushed his son to the Kuwait Specialty Hospital in southern Gaza's Khan Younis, but it was too late.

“He was wrapped up, [but] his head, his clothes, his pants … all of them were soaked in water,” Arqiq told CBC News freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife, holding up the infant's death certificate as he recounted the night’s events.
Earlier this month, heavy rains pummelled parts of Gaza, causing flooding and damaging many shelters. One storm led to the collapse of a sand embankment, killing five people.
Hundreds of people have been living in makeshift tent cities for years, including the Arqiqs, who were displaced from their home in 2023 when Israel's war in Gaza began.
Winter in Gaza brings death, hypothermia and floods

As heavy rains hit the Gaza Strip in the week leading up to the infant's death, many parts of the enclave flooded, leaving people stuck in metres of water with their belongings drenched. For the Arqiq family, that meant the baby's clothing and blankets were soaked and they were unable to fully dry him.
Kinan, the youngest of three children, eventually died of hypothermia — the first death from the condition this season in Gaza.
“My son died from the cold,” Arqiq said. “His mother wanted to nurse him and she found him dead.”
'He was living in very bad conditions'
Dr. Jamal Al-Hams, medical director at the Kuwaiti Hospital, said the infant was dead on arrival. He said the baby had no other underlying medical conditions.
“The cause of death was due to … to the severe, extremely cold weather he was exposed to in his tent,” he said. “He was living in very bad conditions.”
Temperatures in Gaza tend to fall overnight in the winter, where they can hover around eight to 10 C or even as low as seven degrees.
In a press release published on Tuesday, Shaun Hughes, UN World Food Programme country director for Palestine, said Gaza was facing a “deepening” shelter, sanitation and food security crisis.
A displaced Palestinian man stands in a partially flooded tent camp during a rainy day in Gaza City on Nov. 7. (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)
“Winter rains flood makeshift shelters, destroy scarce food supplies and leave displaced families struggling to stay warm and fed,” it reads.

A UN report published in February 2026 stated that at least 11 children had reportedly died of hypothermia that winter. It said the situation “underscores the deadly impact of exposure to cold conditions without adequate shelter.”
In January 2025, the UN reported eight newborns and 74 children died of hypothermia in the prior month alone.

The war began on Oct. 7, 2023, after a Hamas-led attack on Israel killed some 1,200 people, by Israeli tallies, with another some 250 taken hostage. Since then, more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Aid still needed, orgs say
A year into the fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, the flow of aid has improved, but the demand still outstrips supply, humanitarian groups say.
“When you’re in Gaza, it does not feel like a ceasefire,” Hughes said.
The Israeli military still controls about 70 per cent of the Gaza Strip, he said, making it difficult for Palestinians to grow their own food.

“Fishing in the sea is prohibited and also life-threatening," he said, due to risk of gunfire. "Unemployment is over 80 per cent, so without humanitarian assistance, people have little or no alternate means of survival."
A Palestinian lights a fire outside his tent at a tent camp set up inside a school, in Khan Younis, on Nov. 18. (Ramadan Abed/Reuters)

More than 93,000 tents and 8,600 trucks with winter supplies have entered Gaza as part of the Israeli military's winterization plan for the region, the Co-ordination of Government Activities in the Territories subunit posted on X last week.
But many aid groups say it’s still not enough.

"Without proper shelter, without critical relief items, then hypothermia deaths ​will occur," Karl Baker, head of the UN International Organization for Migration's Gaza programme, said on Tuesday, adding that children were particularly vulnerable, since they lose body heat more quickly.
He said the supply of aid has been hindered by lengthy Israeli security checks and crossing closures.
"Gaza is turning into one ​large IDP camp [internally displaced persons]. It ranks as one of the worst I've walked through," he said.

items: Woman, 3 children killed in Gaza after sand embankment collapses onto tents
Tents housing thousands of displaced families flooded in Gaza

blocks.text: Back at the Kuwaiti Hospital, Arqiq carried his son to the hospital's courtyard, where a funeral prayer was held. The little shrouded body lay on a coat on the ground in front of rows of family, friends and passersby lined up to pray before the body was carried to its grave.
“He was like a flower,” Arqiq said, tears rolling down his cheeks.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yasmine Hassan is a producer in CBC's Ottawa bureau. From there, she covers developments inside Gaza and the West Bank related to the Israel-Hamas war. If you have a story idea, send news tips in English or Arabic to yasmine.hassan@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Mohamed El Saife and Reuters

articles.title: Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
articles.summary: A Pentagon budget officer has said the price of the Iran war surpassed $48.3 billion last week. That does not include costs sustained in Iranian attacks on US bases — lawmakers want details the…

image.caption: Iranian missiles and drones have caused billions of dollars in damage to US military infrastructure across the Middle East since the war beganImage: AFP

blocks.text: The cost of the US war in Iran, which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller.
Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered.
Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East.
How much damage has Iran inflicted on US military installations in the Middle East?

According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing.
Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible.
In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who said damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion.
The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion.
Iran launches retaliatory strikes across Gulf region
A war by any name, is still a very expensive undertaking

The Trump administration has variously argued that the war is not a war, that it has been won, and that it will be over soon. There is currently no end in sight and on top of the US military's costs, the global economy is getting pummeled every day as a result of the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which is the direct result of US attacks on the Islamic Republic.

The Trump administration is calling on Congress to pass the Pentagon's $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget — a 40% increase over 2026 — in order to fund America's military. Unlikely prior to the November 3 midterm elections, the prospects of that figure being approved now that Democrats have taken control of both houses of Congress from Republicans would seem nigh impossible.

articles.title: New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz
articles.summary: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz says European leaders could take part in fresh Ukraine talks on "neutral ground." The UK and EU countries have urged a seat at the table in meetings between the…

image.caption: Merz is one of the most pro-Ukraine leaders in EuropeImage: Hannah McKay/REUTERS

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday he believes new talks regarding Russia's invasion of Ukraine with European leaders taking part will occur "soon."
What did Merz say about the next Ukraine talks?

"Of course we are prepared to hold talks with Russia, we have always said this. These talks are now set to take place soon," Merz said after a meeting of Ukraine's allies in Berlin. He did not give a concrete date for the next talks, but said Europe's interests would be represented by Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present at the Coalition of the Willing summit in the German capital, along with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
Merz said the talks including Europe would take place on "neutral ground," such as the United Arab Emirates.

Merz along with other European leaders have been critical of meetings between US, Ukrainian and Russian representatives regarding the conflict, arguing that Europe needs a direct seat at the negotiating table.
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Putin, in talks with Trump, says European leaders invited to Moscow
Russia's invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, with the Trump administration prioritizing an end to the war.

Trump took part in a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Friday, with Trump saying the two leaders would discuss the war in closed-door talks. Putin acknowledged that Europeans want a seat at the table, and said Russia invited European leaders to Moscow.
"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without Europeans," Putin said, while rejecting any military cooperation between Europe and Ukraine.
Merz: 'Yalta format cannot bring peace' to Ukraine
Trump also took part in a historic trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting raised fears that the US, Russia and China are looking to carve up the world into spheres of influence. It drew comparisons with the February 1945 Yalta Conference, where US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Union leader Joseph Stalin discussed Europe's future as Nazi Germany's defeat was imminent in World War II.
Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
Following the Trump-Xi-Putin summit, Merz said a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine. He downplayed the Shenzhen summit between the three leaders as a "photo opportunity."
Merz handed out pieces of the Berlin Wall to leaders at the Coalition of the Willing summit, saying the Yalta structure had brought "oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace."
"This is exactly what Yalta stood for," Merz said.

The Yalta format sought to divide post-war Germany into four zones: US, UK, France and the USSR. This later led to the construction of the Berlin Wall dividing the city into West and East Berlin, with city residents attempting to cross the barrier shot dead by border guards.
Marking the divide: The Berlin Wall Memorial

articles.title: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
articles.summary: Rose, who died in 2024, was given a lifetime ban from the sport for betting on games but was reinstated last year.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.
"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.
The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.
Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.
According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".
The BBC has contacted the Baseball Hall of Fame for comment.
The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.
"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.

MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.

In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.

In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

articles.title: Florida to carry out record-breaking 20th execution of the year
articles.summary:
State to execute man convicted of two counts of first-degree murder while Texas also plans to put a man to death

Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the…

blocks.text: Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist.

Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6pm at Florida state prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, was set to receive a lethal injection about an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the ageing of the US death row population.

Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office in January 1996.

On Thursday, Overton woke up at 5am and remained compliant, a Florida department of corrections spokesperson, Jordan Kirkland, said during a news conference. He did not meet with any visitors or a spiritual adviser.

Florida has carried out more than half the nation’s 37 executions this year under Ron DeSantis, the state’s outgoing Republican governor who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday’s scheduled executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US after Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in October.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
On Thursday, the US supreme court denied a final appeal in the Florida case while an appeal remained pending in the Texas case.
Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence.

The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home in August 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene but initially found no match with samples in the state’s database. But Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities said a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors’ home, and he was charged with their killings.

In the Texas case, Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’s request.
The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his attacker.

Police found the jeweler’s body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents said officers found the jeweler’s safe empty with no sign of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand. The diamonds have never been recovered.
Dennes’s attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs.
Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022.
“I did those things, so I am guilty,” Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor’s filing said.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

articles.title: California probing whether China improperly acquired Nvidia technology
articles.summary: The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure.

blocks.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.
